Signal is whatever you're after

Signal-to-noise isn't about dialogue in particular. It's the sound you want against everything else. Record the phone as an effect and the actor becomes noise. Record the traffic as ambience and the phone is the problem.

Gain moves both together

Turning the gain up makes the signal louder and the noise louder by exactly the same amount. Only moving the mic, aiming it, or switching things off changes the gap between them. Auto gain makes it worse, turning itself up in every quiet gap.

Directional isn't a zoom

A shotgun narrows what it hears, it doesn't reach further. It's the right tool for one voice or one prop. For ambience you want the opposite: an omni hears the whole space evenly. Sounds arriving off-axis also come through duller.

A teaching model, not a measurement. Levels follow the inverse square law and textbook first-order patterns, and sounds coming in off-axis are dulled as they would be on a real directional mic. The shotgun is a simplified mid-to-high frequency shape, real ones are wider in the bass. Null depth is capped at −25 dB, as real mics never fully cancel. Room reflections aren't modelled. dBFS levels assume a typical mic and preamp, and auto gain is modelled on a camera's automatic gain control.
